met-437980.title: Cypresses
met-437980.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
met-437980.body:
The trees occupy almost the full height of the canvas. Small changes in the direction of the strokes make their dark forms feel dense and restless. The sky remains visible around them, while the lower vegetation brings the eye back towards the ground.

In June 1889, Vincent wrote about his wish to paint cypresses. Their proportions reminded him of an obelisk, and their dark green presented a particular challenge against the surrounding light.

This painting belongs to his close study of a subject he continued to develop. It later appeared at the Salon des Indépendants in 1890.

Begin with the difficulty he described: how can a very dark tree remain distinct, varied and alive within a bright landscape? The question connects his written ambitions with the physical marks on the canvas.

stories.title: A Problem in Dark Green
stories.body: Vincent's discussion of cypresses is unusually specific about proportion and colour. He was interested in finding a convincing painted form for a tree whose darkness could be difficult to handle. That practical problem offers a grounded starting point for this canvas. As you move closer, ask how many kinds of green you can distinguish and how those variations prevent the mass of foliage from becoming a single flat shape.
stories.prompt: Find a light stroke inside the dark foliage. What does it change?

stories.title: A Vertical Study

Compare that arrangement with the horizontal wheatfield in entry 23. In one, the tree becomes a large presence close to the viewer. In the other, the eye travels across a much wider field. The comparison makes format part of the story of looking.

met-437998.title: Olive Trees
met-437998.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
met-437998.collectionCredit: The Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg Collection, Gift of Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg, 1998, Bequest of Walter H. Annenberg, 2002
met-437998.body:
The trunks turn through a field of broken colour. Short strokes travel across the ground, then collect into the trees' foliage. The orchard offers a place to look repeatedly, with shifting light and different relationships between earth, leaves and sky.

In November 1889, Vincent was discussing the religious pictures of Gauguin and Bernard. He responded critically and described his own work among olive trees in clear, cold weather. His letters place the grove within a continuing conversation about how pictures should be made.

The Met identifies this canvas with that November campaign.  Here, a walk into an orchard becomes part of a working argument: attend to a place, test what you see, and develop a painted response through repeated attempts.

stories.title: An Argument Among Artists
stories.body: The letters show a disagreement that had subjects, names and dates. Vincent questioned the religious compositions sent or described by his friends and explained his own attention to olive groves.  That exchange helps us situate the painting within an artistic network. It does not require us to turn every tree into a symbol of the argument. The correspondence records his position at a particular moment, within a practice that also included memory, invention and copies.
stories.prompt: Which details suggest close attention to the forms of these particular trees?

stories.title: Work in Cold Sunshine
stories.body: On 26 November, Vincent described working in the groves during bright, cold days and developing a group of five canvases.  Weather affected the conditions of work and the effects available to observe. The precise hour represented by this particular painting is not established here. Instead, compare the ground and foliage: how do the strokes bring different surfaces into the same light? The question keeps the written working conditions beside the visible painting.

stories.title: Recognising a Country Through Its Trees
stories.body: Vincent compared the importance of olive trees and cypresses in the south with the familiar willows of his native country.  The comparison makes the landscape a process of recognition. A tree could give a place its character, while learning its forms required time. This exhibition follows that attention through several works. Looking across them, notice what repeats and what changes without assuming that every return to a subject carried the same emotional meaning.
stories.prompt: Compare an olive trunk here with a willow in an early drawing. What kinds of movement do their forms invite?

met-437984.title: The Lullaby (Augustine Roulin)
met-437984.catalogueTitle: La Berceuse (Woman Rocking a Cradle; Augustine-Alix Pellicot Roulin, 1851–1930)
met-437984.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
met-437984.collectionCredit: The Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg Collection, Gift of Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg, 1996, Bequest of Walter H. Annenberg, 2002
met-437984.body:
Augustine Roulin holds the cord of a cradle outside the frame. The portrait combines her seated presence with an action we complete in our imagination. This canvas is one of five versions of the subject. According to the Met, it is the version Augustine chose for herself.

That choice gives the story another voice, even though we do not have her own account of it. She had an opportunity to judge the pictures and select one.

Vincent later discussed versions as possible gifts to other artists.  Their circulation could involve sitters, friends and recipients, each with a different relationship to the image. In this exhibition, Augustine's choice keeps our attention on the person whose likeness became the series' centre.

stories.title: The Sitter as a Viewer
stories.body: The Met records that Augustine selected this version and that Vincent approved of her judgement.  We can recognise an act of preference without inventing her explanation for it. Perhaps you would choose differently. When comparing versions, begin with a detail you can name: a line around the hands, the relationship of the hair to the background, or a change in the surface. Your response is yours; hers remains partly beyond our reach.
stories.prompt: Which detail would you use to explain your preference for a version?

stories.title: Work Beyond the Frame
stories.body: The cord is a small object carrying much of the subject's action. Follow it through the hands, across the dress and towards the edge. The cradle itself is absent from the composition.  This cropping asks the viewer to imagine a larger room and a repeated movement. Our reading begins with that ordinary action. It leaves room for Augustine's individual presence alongside the broader associations of care suggested by the title.
stories.prompt: Cover the cord with your hand on the screen. How much of the story remains visible?

stories.title: A Portrait That Could Travel
stories.body: Vincent's May letter proposed sending versions of La Berceuse to Gauguin and Bernard as tokens of friendship.  Those proposals belong to the series and are not an ownership history for this particular canvas. The distinction matters. A painting can participate in an artist's wider plans while still having a specific route through owners and collections. Here, the series link opens those plans; this object's information page preserves its separate identity.
stories.prompt: What changes when you think of a portrait as something given to another person?

seriesReading.title: La Berceuse: A Series
seriesReading.labelTitle: A Picture That Might Comfort Someone
seriesReading.body:
Augustine Roulin sits with a cord in her hands. The cradle it moves remains outside the picture. Her portrait became a repeated project, carried across five canvases during the months around Vincent's crisis in Arles.

Writing to Theo on 28 January 1889, Vincent imagined a further setting for the image: the cabin of a fishing boat. A sailor looking at it might remember the experience of being rocked and hearing a lullaby. This was a hope for what a picture could offer another person.

He also considered how the portrait would look between two paintings of sunflowers. Here, that arrangement can be explored as a documented proposal.

The story gives us several ways into the work: a woman who sat for him, an action extending beyond the frame, and an imagined audience far from Arles.

stories.title: An Audience at Sea
stories.body: Vincent's imagined sailors were people facing danger and isolation. His letter connects their circumstances with an ordinary memory of childhood care. The painting's possible effect concerned recognition, the feeling that an image could recall a familiar rhythm. We can follow this wish without assuming that the work ever reached the cabin he described. The letter preserves an intention; the eventual experiences of viewers remain open.
stories.prompt: Follow the cord from Augustine's hands to the edge of the canvas. What happens beyond the picture?

stories.title: Five Attempts at One Subject
stories.body: A series gives a portrait a different kind of duration. Augustine's pose returns, while colour, surface and small details invite comparison. Each canvas has its own history and present location. In this exhibition, the repeated subject becomes an opportunity to look at decisions: where a contour becomes firmer, how a floral background approaches the figure, and how much visual weight rests in the hands. These comparisons are looking exercises, not a ranking supplied by Vincent.
stories.prompt: Compare one small area across two identified versions, keeping the image scale the same.

stories.title: Between the Sunflowers
stories.body: In a letter dated about 23 May 1889, Vincent drew a proposed arrangement with the portrait at the centre and sunflowers at either side. He explained the interaction of their colours and also discussed giving versions to fellow artists. The arrangement links decoration with exchange and friendship. Our digital reconstruction lets you test the relationship while keeping its status visible: a proposal recorded in a letter, recreated for this exhibition.
stories.prompt: Look first at the portrait alone, then with the two yellow panels beside it. Where does your attention settle?

highlight-33.title: The Starry Night
highlight-33.institution: The Museum of Modern Art, New York
highlight-33.collectionCredit: Acquired through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest
highlight-33.body:
Vincent wrote about looking out before sunrise and seeing a large morning star. A later June letter mentions a new study of a starry sky.  These are traces of looking and working, attached to particular moments in his correspondence.

On the canvas, the sky fills most of the space. A cypress rises close to the viewer, and a village gathers below the hills. MoMA explains the scene through a combination of observation, memory and imagination; the village is constructed, with a church spire recalling Dutch architecture.

The picture allows the distant and the remembered to occupy one place. We can approach its making through the painter's choices while remaining careful about what the image can tell us about his health. A painted sky is not a clinical record.

stories.title: Something Seen Before Sunrise
stories.body: The morning-star passage gives the story a time of day and an act of attention.  It does not describe the finished painting in every detail. Move between the short written observation and the much larger image: Vincent had to decide what to retain, enlarge and bring into relation with other forms. This card follows that passage from looking to composing without claiming that a single instant supplies a complete explanation of the work.
stories.prompt: Locate the brightest star-like form. How does the space around it make it appear large?

stories.title: A Village Brought Into the View
stories.body: MoMA identifies the village as an invented part of the composition and connects its spire with architecture familiar from Vincent's Dutch background.  The small buildings give the eye a place to settle below the moving sky. In our reading, their scale helps the landscape feel inhabitable. That effect belongs to the picture as we encounter it. It should remain distinct from a claim that this is an exact map of Saint-Rémy seen from his window.
stories.prompt: Compare the village spire with the cypress. How do these two upward forms organise the scene?

stories.title: A Painter Looking Back at His Work
stories.body: Vincent later discussed the risks of moving too far from observed subjects. The scholarly notes to his November letter associate part of this discussion with The Starry Night and point to other letters in which his response was more positive.  His judgement developed through correspondence. Let that changing assessment remain part of the exhibition: an artist could make an ambitious picture, reconsider its decisions, and continue testing his practice.
stories.prompt: Which part seems most closely observed, and which seems most deliberately arranged?

met-436536.title: Women Picking Olives
met-436536.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
met-436536.collectionCredit: The Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg Collection, Gift of Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg, 1995, Bequest of Walter H. Annenberg, 2002
met-436536.body:
Figures work beneath the olive trees. Their gestures bring a repeated human activity into the orchard, joining the bent trunks and the ground's patterned surface.

Vincent developed this subject in three versions. The Met identifies its canvas as the most resolved of the group and records that he intended it for his mother and sister.

That intended destination gives the scene a relationship beyond the place it depicts. A picture of southern work could become something to share with family elsewhere. In this exhibition, we can follow that connection without inventing the recipients' response.

Look at the small intervals between bodies, branches and earth. The story unfolds through ordinary movement: reach, bend, gather, and begin again. These are looking prompts offered by the exhibition, grounded in the figures visible before us.

stories.title: A Subject Developed Three Times
stories.body: The Met distinguishes an initial study from nature, a second version made in the studio, and this further treatment.  The sequence invites us to consider how a subject changes through repeated work. Place identified versions side by side and choose one element to compare. The distance between figures, the balance of the trees or the rhythm of a patch of ground may reveal decisions that a single image cannot show. Avoid treating the sequence as an automatic progress from failure to success.
stories.prompt: Compare where the figures sit within each composition. How does their spacing change your sense of the grove?

stories.title: Following the Work of Hands
stories.body: Begin with one figure, then follow the direction of the arm towards the surrounding branches. Move to another figure and repeat the exercise. Their positions create a sequence your eye can travel through, although the painting fixes every gesture in place. Our reading connects that visual sequence with the labour named in the title. It does not tell us who these workers were, what they earned, or what they felt on a particular day. Those questions require other evidence.
stories.prompt: Which gesture makes the relationship between a person and a tree clearest?

stories.title: A Friend Could Still Approve
stories.body: The museum also reports Vincent's statement that Gauguin liked a related drawing.  That detail allows a more particular account of their relationship. Disagreement over artistic methods could coexist with an approving response to a specific work. This exhibition preserves both kinds of exchange. A small piece of correspondence can complicate a broad biographical label, while leaving the exact reasons for Gauguin's approval to the surviving evidence.
stories.prompt: What might a drawing of this subject preserve especially clearly: gesture, spacing, or the shape of the trees?

met-436536.evidence:

Curatorial reading: Repeated labour and the idea of a gift connect place with family.

Unknown: The workers' identities and the recipients' precise reaction. An intended gift is not, by itself, proof of its arrival.

highlight-37.title: Irises (garden)
highlight-37.institution: The J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles
highlight-37.body:
During his first week at Saint-Paul-de-Mausole, Vincent began painting irises in the hospital garden. He considered the canvas a study.  A letter of 9 May mentions violet irises among the work already under way.

The flowers are close to us. Leaves cross one another, petals turn in different directions, and the composition continues beyond its edges. The space offers enough variation to keep looking.

The colours have a history of their own. Getty's conservation research shows that the flowers' present blue appearance was altered by the fading of red pigment in an original violet mixture.

Here, the garden enters the story through attention and material evidence. We see the image Vincent worked on, and we learn that even a familiar painting has changed during the time it has survived.

stories.title: A First Week of Work
stories.body: The hospital garden provided a subject near the place where Vincent was staying. His first letter from Saint-Rémy describes work already begun and his hope that his capacity for work would return.  The hope belongs to that letter's moment. It should not be converted into a promise of permanent recovery. At the painting, we can follow a manageable task: attend to one plant, then another, and bring their forms into a shared space.
stories.prompt: Find two flowers turned in different directions. What changes in their outlines?

stories.title: Looking at a Surface That Has Changed
stories.body: Getty researchers found evidence of the light-sensitive red pigment geranium lake in the paint. Its fading helps explain why flowers Vincent described as violet now look blue.  A technical image can show evidence invisible in an ordinary reproduction. A colour reconstruction can then test how the composition might once have appeared. Keep those functions separate: analysis identifies material traces; reconstruction proposes an appearance based on them. Neither is a photograph taken in 1889.
stories.prompt: Imagine more violet among the flowers. How might its relationship with the surrounding warm colours change?

stories.title: A Study Reaches an Exhibition
stories.body: Theo submitted Irises to the Salon des Indépendants in September 1889.  The painting therefore reached an audience during Vincent's lifetime. In this exhibition, that event follows the garden story: an image made through close attention became a work other people could encounter elsewhere. A reception panel may later add documented reactions. For now, the dated event is enough to show that its history had already extended beyond the hospital grounds.

met-436528.title: Irises (in a vase)
met-436528.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
met-436528.body:
In May 1890, Vincent painted four ambitious bouquets before leaving Saint-Rémy. This vase of irises belonged to that group.

The flowers have been gathered into an interior arrangement. Leaves and petals spread across the wide canvas, held together by the vase and the limited space around it. The image gives us another way to follow a subject he had already studied in the garden.

In a June letter to Willemien, Vincent recalled the flower paintings and their intended colour relationships.  The colours we see today have also changed through the fading of red pigments.

Here, a familiar subject marks a new working situation. The flowers were cut, arranged and painted close to the end of his stay. Their presence provides a concrete point of entry into those days.

stories.title: Four Bouquets, Several Decisions
stories.body: The group contained two paintings of irises and two of roses, with different formats and colour relationships.  A comparison can begin with practical choices: how much space a bouquet occupies, where the vase sits, and how flowers meet the edge. Follow one decision across the group. The exhibition presents the series as a set of working experiments, leaving claims about a single emotional message to sources that can support them.

stories.body: Vincent's June account describes violet irises against a pink background, with a gentle relationship between the colours.  The Met explains that fugitive red pigments have altered the appearance of both flowers and background.  Read the letter beside the present image and allow the difference to remain visible. A reconstruction would require more than a general tint: separate areas changed differently, and the original balance cannot be recovered by applying one filter.

stories.body: The Met records that this painting belonged to Vincent's mother until her death in 1907.  Ownership keeps a family relationship attached to the object's later life. It does not tell us precisely where she hung it or how she spoke about it. The exhibition can show the confirmed link and then let the picture stand as something preserved. A painting's survival may involve people whose choices receive less attention than the artist's.

met-336327.medium: Brush and oils over black chalk on pink laid paper
met-336327.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
met-336327.body:
A corridor extends through the image. Repeated openings and arches carry the eye inward, while changes in light make sections of the passage distinct.

Vincent made this work on paper in September 1889 and sent it to Theo to show his surroundings at Saint-Rémy.  It belongs to an exchange between brothers as well as to the record of a building.

The materials are specific: black chalk under drawing, brush-applied oils and pink laid paper.  Look closely at the relationship between drawn structure and painted surface.

For this exhibition, the passage gives the story a place to inhabit. Its architecture can feel enclosing, distant or quiet to different viewers. Those impressions remain responses to an image, held alongside what the object record can tell us about its making and purpose.

stories.title: Looking Down a Passage
stories.body: Begin near the bottom of the image and trace one architectural edge into the distance. Repeated elements help establish a route for the eye. The spaces between them become smaller as they recede. Our looking exercise asks how that arrangement affects your experience of the corridor. A visitor may feel drawn forward, kept at a distance or made aware of the enclosing walls. None of these responses, on its own, establishes the state of mind of the person who painted it.
stories.prompt: Which line carries your eye furthest into the building?

sources.label: The Met, Corridor in the Asylum

stories.title: Colour on Paper
stories.body: This is a work in oils on paper over a black-chalk drawing.  The support belongs to its identity. Look for places where a drawn contour remains active beside a painted area, and for places where the surface appears more open. The image offers a chance to compare drawing and painting as overlapping activities. Any claim about a particular mark's material should be checked against a technical record, since a screen image cannot identify every substance reliably.
stories.prompt: Find an edge that feels drawn and an area that feels brushed. How do they work together?

sources.label: The Met, Corridor in the Asylum

stories.title: An Image Sent to Someone Else
stories.body: The Met identifies the work as something sent to Theo to convey Vincent's environment.  That purpose gives the corridor a recipient. The artist selected a view, worked it into an image and made it available to someone living elsewhere. In this exhibition, the picture joins a wider story of correspondence: words and images helped maintain contact. We do not reconstruct Theo's exact response unless a surviving letter can establish it.
stories.prompt: If you wanted to show someone the place where you were staying, which view would you choose?

sources.label: The Met, Corridor in the Asylum

met-336327.evidence:
Documented by the museum: Date, materials and the purpose of showing Theo the surroundings.

Curatorial reading: Repetition, distance and the work's status as a communicated view shape this presentation.

Unknown: The exact feelings experienced during its making or a diagnosis encoded in its perspective. Architecture depicted in a painting should not be treated as a medical test.

met-436526.title: First Steps, after Millet
met-436526.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
met-436526.collectionCredit: Gift of George N. and Helen M. Richard, 1964
met-436526.body:
A child moves between two adults. Arms reach across the small space, and the surrounding garden gives the action an everyday setting.

Vincent worked from a photograph of Millet's composition sent by Theo. He used a grid to transfer its structure onto canvas, then developed the colour.

In correspondence, he compared interpreting another artist's work with performing music. A composition could be received, studied and given an individual rendering.

This painting therefore carries several kinds of contact: with an admired predecessor, with the brother who supplied the image, and with a subject of care and tentative movement. The family's action belongs to Millet's source. Vincent's work gives us a way to follow how that image was made newly present through another painter's materials and decisions.

stories.title: Theo Sends an Image
stories.body: A photograph made a distant composition available for work in Saint-Rémy.  The source could be kept nearby, studied and transferred without standing before Millet's original. This card places reproduction within the practical story of making art. A picture sent through a family network became a working resource. Comparing the photograph with the painting helps us see what Vincent retained from Millet and where colour gives the composition a new presence.
stories.prompt: Compare a source reproduction with the painting. Which large shapes remain easiest to recognise?

sources.label: The Met, First Steps, after Millet

stories.title: Transferring a Structure
stories.body: The Met records the use of a squared photograph to transfer the composition.  A grid helps move relationships from one scale to another: the position of a head, the span between arms, or the edge of a garden bed. Our digital overlay demonstrates that principle. It is an explanatory tool, not a tracing recovered from the painting. Turn it off again to see how the figures and surrounding space hold together without the guide.
stories.prompt: Which relationship would be hardest to preserve while enlarging the image?

sources.label: The Met, First Steps, after Millet

stories.title: Playing Another Artist's Composition
stories.body: In September 1889, Vincent explained how copying could involve a personal interpretation, as in musical performance. Working from black-and-white sources, he developed colour and described the activity as instructive and at times consoling.  The letter concerns his broader practice of copies and predates this January canvas. It gives us a method to look for: a retained composition and a new arrangement of colour within it.
stories.prompt: Choose a colour relationship that could not be supplied by a black-and-white photograph alone.

Unproven: The child stands for the painter's own lost future, or the adults are portraits of a family he personally wished to have.

vgm-s0176v1962.title: Almond Blossom
vgm-s0176v1962.institution: Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)
vgm-s0176v1962.storyGroup: A New Member of the Family
vgm-s0176v1962.body:
A new child entered the family while Vincent was in Saint-Rémy. Theo and Jo named their son Vincent Willem.

On 19 February 1890, Vincent wrote to his mother that he had begun a painting for the baby: large branches of white almond blossom against blue, intended for Theo and Jo's bedroom.

The branches spread across the canvas with little indication of the ground below. Flowers, buds and the spaces between them make the sky part of the design.

By June, Vincent reported that the picture hung above the piano in the family's apartment.  The work had a destination in an ordinary room. In this exhibition, that placement brings its later fame back to a particular relationship: an uncle making something for a child and the people who would raise him.

stories.title: A Reason to Begin
stories.body: Vincent's February letter gives this painting a clearly stated purpose. He wanted to make it for the new baby and described its subject and intended place in the parents' room.  The story needs no invented speech from the child or a claim that painting removed all difficulties from the artist's life. The gift is already meaningful as an action: selecting a subject, beginning work and planning where the finished image might live.
stories.prompt: Which part of the composition makes the branches feel close to you?

sources.label: Letter 855, to his mother, 19 February 1890
sources.kind: Artist’s letter · scholarly edition and editorial notes

stories.title: Branches Across the Picture Plane
stories.body: The Van Gogh Museum connects the subject, firm outlines and placement of the branches with Japanese printmaking.  The composition offers a focused exercise in looking: follow a branch as it crosses the sky, then attend to the empty shape beside it. Flowers are also organised through the blue spaces around them. This reading concerns the arrangement of the image. It does not require the branches to represent a coded account of Vincent's health.
stories.prompt: Find a blue shape enclosed by branches. What happens when you look at that space as a form?

stories.title: Above the Piano
stories.body: In his June letter to Willemien, Vincent reported the painting's position above the piano.  The detail lets us follow the gift from intention to a documented domestic setting. This exhibition uses the reported placement as a small part of the painting's history. A diagram may help visitors picture the relationship of wall, instrument and canvas, as long as it is labelled a schematic. The apartment's precise appearance is not established by this sentence alone.
stories.prompt: How might a picture feel different when it is seen in a room used every day?

met-849056.title: Portrait of Doctor Gachet or Man with a Pipe
met-849056.catalogueTitle: Portrait of Doctor Gachet or Man with a Pipe
met-849056.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
met-849056.collectionCredit: Purchase, Fletcher Fund, William R. Drexler Sr. and Violet Drexler Bequest, The Elisha Whittelsey Collection, The Elisha Whittelsey Fund, and The Derald H. Ruttenberg Foundation, in honor of Nadine M. Orenstein and Charles and Jessie Price Gifts, 2021
met-849056.storyGroup: A Portrait, a Printer and an Unfinished Plan
met-849056.body:
The face at the centre of this small print belongs to the world of Auvers. Its title leaves room for two descriptions: Doctor Gachet, or a man with a pipe. The print holds a likeness together with the practical question of how an image can be made and circulated.

The Metropolitan Museum identifies Paul-Ferdinand Gachet as the printer. The folded sheet also preserves an inscription connected with an artist's proof. Vincent was therefore involved in more than the act of drawing. The image passed through a working relationship that included a sitter, a plate, an impression and a person with access to a press.

On 17 June 1890, Vincent wrote to Theo about the possibility of making several more etchings of southern subjects, with Gachet printing them. He imagined a small group of works and mentioned the possibility of Gauguin's participation. The proposal remained incomplete.

This object asks us to look at reproduction as part of artistic practice. One etched composition can survive in several impressions. Each impression has its own paper, inscriptions, condition and history. The exhibition keeps those levels separate while following the plan that briefly connected portraiture, friendship and printmaking.

stories.title: One Plate, Several Impressions
stories.body:
The Metropolitan Museum catalogues this object as an etching and identifies Gachet as printer.  An etching plate can produce more than one impression. The title of the composition and the physical history of a particular sheet therefore belong to different layers of information.

Each impression is a separate object. Paper tone, margins, inscriptions and the density of the lines can differ from one sheet to another. These details belong to the print's material history and help distinguish an individual impression from the image shared across the edition. A comparison begins with the identity of each sheet.
stories.prompt: Which marks seem to belong to the etched composition, and which belong to the later life of this sheet?

sources.label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Portrait of Doctor Gachet or Man with a Pipe

stories.title: Gachet at the Press
stories.body:
The museum names Paul-Ferdinand Gachet as printer.  This detail changes the scale of the story. The print is not only a picture of a person. It is also an object shaped by a working process in which printing knowledge mattered.

The identity of the printer does not prove that every decision was shared equally, and it does not allow us to reconstruct a conversation that has not survived. It does give the object a second human presence. A portrait of a doctor carries the trace of a printer who helped turn the image into a repeatable form.
stories.prompt: If the image were printed again, which qualities would you want to preserve: the face, the pipe, the pressure of the line, or the unevenness of the impression?

sources.label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Portrait of Doctor Gachet or Man with a Pipe

stories.title: Six Further Etchings
stories.body:
In a letter to Theo, Vincent proposed making about six more etchings of southern subjects. He described Gachet as the person who could print them and considered whether Gauguin might participate.  The letter records an intention and a working plan. It does not document a completed series.

The proposed group opens a small window onto Vincent's late practice. He was still considering how images might move between artists, techniques and audiences. A plan that remained unfinished can still be part of the history of an artwork when the plan is clearly labelled as such.
stories.prompt: What does this print make possible that a single oil painting cannot?

Curatorial reading: The print joins portraiture with the practical infrastructure of making and circulating images.

Unknown: The exact printing date of this impression, the full sequence of impressions, the extent of Gachet's decisions, and whether the proposed group was ever begun beyond the surviving evidence.

hiroshima-f776.title: Daubigny's Garden (Hiroshima version)
hiroshima-f776.storyGroup: Admiration, Versions and a Garden in a Letter
hiroshima-f776.body:
Vincent had admired the French landscape painter Charles-François Daubigny for many years. In Auvers, he painted the artist's garden as a subject that carried both a real place and a history of looking.

The garden does not arrive in the exhibition as a single, isolated image. Vincent made more than one version. A small study in Amsterdam belongs to the same subject, while the Hiroshima Museum of Art preserves a wider canvas. A letter of 23 July 1890 contains a garden sketch that scholars connect with the Hiroshima painting. The sketch gives the work a place within correspondence as well as within the landscape of Auvers.

The surviving material also leaves questions open. A black cat appears in the letter sketch and is said in the scholarly note to have been painted out later. The available evidence does not establish when this happened or who made the change. The exhibition shows the story as a sequence of observations, attributions and uncertainties.

To look at this garden is to look at a late subject through several forms: a place, a study, a broad canvas, and a drawing shared with his brother in a letter. Each form preserves a different part of the work's history.

stories.title: An Admirer’s Visit
stories.body:
Daubigny was an important artistic reference for Vincent. The garden subject belongs to this long admiration, although the surviving sources do not give us a complete account of every visit or every conversation connected with the painting.

Use the title as an invitation to look closely at the garden's structure. Search for the boundary between cultivated space and open distance. Ask how a garden can carry the presence of an artist who is absent from the scene.
stories.prompt: Which part of the garden feels most deliberately arranged?

stories.title: A Sketch Travels in a Letter
stories.body:
On 23 July 1890, Vincent sent Theo a letter containing garden sketches. The editorial notes identify one sketch with the Hiroshima canvas, F776 / JH2104.  The sketch is not a replacement for the painting. It is evidence of how the subject could be described, planned or shared through correspondence.

The sketch and the canvas preserve two ways of recording the garden. Their shapes, proportions and arrangement of plants make comparison possible. The connection between them is an identification made by the editors of Vincent's letters. That attribution is part of the evidence: the sketch gives us access to his correspondence, while the editors explain which surviving canvas they believe it represents.
stories.prompt: What survives when a wide landscape is reduced to a small sketch?

sources.label: Vincent van Gogh, Letter 902, 23 July 1890
sources.kind: Artist’s letter · scholarly edition and editorial notes

stories.title: Keeping the Versions Separate
stories.body:
The Hiroshima canvas and the Van Gogh Museum's small Amsterdam study are related works. They are separate objects. The Amsterdam page gives the small study a June 1890 date and records a striped tea towel and a pink ground whose appearance has changed over time. Those conservation details belong to the Amsterdam object and should not be transferred to the Hiroshima canvas.

Moving between the small study and the wide canvas changes our sense of the garden. A near-square format gathers the view into a compact space; the broad canvas carries the eye across a longer stretch of vegetation. Each work has its own support, dimensions and history. Their differences show how a place could remain a subject of attention across several acts of painting.
stories.prompt: What changes when the garden expands from a near-square study to a long horizontal field of vision?

Curatorial reading: A garden becomes a meeting point for admiration, place, repeated working and correspondence.

Unknown: The exact making sequence of the versions, the timing and reason for the black cat's removal, and whether every visual difference can be assigned to Vincent's own hand.

highlight-42.title: The Church at Auvers
highlight-42.body:
The church rises from a low viewpoint, its walls divided into strong colour and its roof gathered beneath a blue sky. The composition looks towards the rear of the building. The missing front entrance belongs to the chosen view. It does not provide a complete explanation of Vincent's relationship to religion.

On 5 June 1890, Vincent described the painting to Willemien. He mentioned cobalt, violet and orange, and connected the Auvers church with the old church tower at Nuenen.  The letter brings an earlier landscape into the later one. A building in Auvers becomes part of a personal history of places, memories and repeated subjects.

The church is familiar enough to recognise and unfamiliar enough to remain unsettled. Its curved lines do not settle into a single architectural rhythm. The surrounding paths and grass hold the building in place while the colour keeps the surface active.

This work belongs to the documented life of Auvers. Its meaning can be approached through colour, viewpoint, correspondence and earlier memory. It should not be reduced to a diagnosis or to a single story about belief.

stories.title: Cobalt, Violet and Orange
stories.body:
Vincent's letter to Willemien names the colours he associated with the painting: cobalt blue, violet and orange.  The letter helps us attend to the work through his own description while leaving the whole painting open to direct looking.

The colour relationships Vincent named in his letter remain visible in the painting. A named pigment is a material and visual clue: it helps us follow what he chose to describe. His words leave room for further looking, and for responses that reach beyond the details he recorded.
stories.prompt: Where does the eye move when the blue sky meets the violet architecture and orange roof?

sources.label: Vincent van Gogh, Letter 879, 5 June 1890

stories.title: Looking from the Rear
stories.body:
The official French title specifies a view of the church from the rear or apse side.  This wording gives the viewpoint a precise architectural description. It does not establish why Vincent chose it.

A plan or rotating model can help visitors understand the direction of looking. Label the model as a reconstruction of viewpoint, not as a reconstruction of Vincent's walk or intention. The rear view can be studied as a formal choice before it is connected to broader interpretations.
stories.prompt: Which architectural lines make the building appear to turn or lean?

stories.title: Remembering Nuenen
stories.body:
In the June 1890 letter, Vincent linked the Auvers church with the old church tower at Nuenen.  The relationship is documented in his words. It does not mean that the two paintings are visual copies or that the later building carries only one memory.

The earlier Nuenen church pictures offer another setting for architecture, horizon and surrounding ground. Vincent's letter connects the two places through memory. Looking across the works, we can follow that association and examine how his handling of a church changed with its setting and his practice.
stories.prompt: What changes when the same kind of building is remembered in a different landscape?

vgm-s0106v1962.title: Wheatfield under Thunderclouds
vgm-s0106v1962.collectionCredit: Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)
vgm-s0106v1962.storyGroup: A Landscape Held Between Weather and Words
vgm-s0106v1962.labelTitle: A Wide Field Under a Changing Sky
vgm-s0106v1962.body:
The field stretches across the canvas in a long horizontal band. Above it, clouds gather and open across a dark sky. The landscape offers very little shelter. Its scale gives the viewer room to move through the image, while its compressed height keeps the ground close to the horizon.

The Van Gogh Museum places the painting among the wheatfields Vincent completed around Auvers in the last weeks of his life. In a letter to Theo and Jo, he described sadness and extreme loneliness, then also wrote about what he considered healthy and fortifying in the countryside.  These words belong to the same late period. They do not function as a private caption written for this canvas.

The unusual elongated format emphasises the breadth of the scene. Two broad horizontal zones carry most of the composition: earth below and sky above. The painting holds weather and human language in the same space. It allows us to read the landscape through a documented letter while continuing to look at what the paint itself does.

The work remains a landscape before it becomes a symbol. Its clouds can be studied as forms, its field as a surface, and its scale as a decision made during the final weeks at Auvers.

stories.title: A Wide Surface to Work Across
stories.body:
The museum describes the elongated format as unusual and connects it with the grandeur of the landscape.  The format changes the physical rhythm of looking. The eye travels laterally across the field instead of moving through a tall vertical scene.

Trace the horizon from one edge to the other. Notice where the brushwork thickens, thins or changes direction. The width gives these small changes a long surface across which to unfold. Looking at their rhythm keeps us close to the material decisions that shaped the view.
stories.prompt: Does your eye move across the field, up into the sky, or back and forth between the two?

sources.label: Van Gogh Museum, Wheatfield under Thunderclouds

stories.title: Read the Whole Passage
stories.body:
The Van Gogh Museum quotes Vincent's words about sadness and extreme loneliness, together with his description of the countryside as healthy and fortifying.  The two statements belong beside one another. The letter preserves a complicated account of the moment, with distress and a sustaining experience of landscape occupying the same passage.

The letter was addressed to Theo and Jo around 10 July 1890. It speaks about a group of paintings and the surrounding countryside. Its language offers a context for looking at this canvas, while leaving the connection between an individual sentence and an individual painting open. Vincent's words preserve several feelings within the same account of his work.
stories.prompt: What in the painting supports a sense of openness? What resists it?

stories.title: A Sky Without a Diagnosis
stories.body:
The sky is dark and active. Visitors may experience it as threatening, expansive, heavy or simply atmospheric. Those responses belong to looking. They do not establish a medical fact about Vincent's state.

Begin with what is visible: the breadth of the field, the weight of the sky and the movement of the brushwork. The letter then brings Vincent's own language into the encounter. A description of colour or weather and an account of a person's experience answer different questions. Holding both in view gives us a fuller encounter with the painting, without asking every cloud to carry a biographical meaning.
stories.prompt: Which description stays closest to what you can see: weight, movement, distance, pressure or something else?

vgm-s0149v1962.title: Wheatfield with Crows
vgm-s0149v1962.collectionCredit: Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)
vgm-s0149v1962.body:
A broad field opens beneath a deep blue sky. Three paths enter the wheat and divide the surface into directions that do not settle into a single route. Dark birds cross the sky. Their shapes are clear enough to attract attention and open enough to invite interpretation.

For many years, the painting has been described as Vincent's last work. The Van Gogh Museum cautions against that claim. Other paintings were made in Auvers after or around this moment, and the evidence does not provide a secure final sequence based on visual drama alone.

A late letter to Theo and Jo describes loneliness, sadness and the countryside's sustaining qualities in relation to a group of wheatfield paintings.  The words belong to the period. They do not turn the birds into a coded message or prove that the scene records a planned farewell.

This painting carries a large afterlife of interpretation. The exhibition places those interpretations beside the record of what can be established. Visitors can look at the branching paths and the moving birds while keeping the historical claim at the correct level of certainty.

stories.title: The Last-Painting Claim
stories.body:
The Van Gogh Museum says that Wheatfield with Crows is often regarded as Vincent's very last painting, then identifies that view as incorrect because other works followed.  The correction matters because a familiar phrase can shape everything seen afterwards.

The phrase “last painting” belongs to the work's later reputation. It encourages viewers to search every bird and path for a farewell. The museum's correction changes that encounter: the picture takes its place among several works from Auvers, and its place in the exact sequence requires historical evidence. A story repeated around a painting can become part of its history even when that story needs correction.
stories.prompt: How does your reading change when the phrase “last painting” is removed from the label?

sources.label: Van Gogh Museum, Wheatfield with Crows

stories.title: Birds and Paths
stories.body:
The birds appear as dark forms against the sky, and the paths divide the field. These features are visible. Their symbolic meanings are not fixed by the picture itself. A reading of birds as death omens, paths as blocked choices or the field as a direct record of the shooting site belongs to later interpretation unless supported by a specific source.

Begin with the painted forms: the low dark marks of the birds, the branching paths and the bands of field and sky. These shapes guide the eye before any symbolic explanation is added. When a bird becomes an omen or a path becomes a life choice, we have moved from description into interpretation. Recognising that movement helps us keep the visible painting and the stories told around it in view.
stories.prompt: Count the directions in the field. Which path does your eye follow first, and why?

sources.label: Van Gogh Museum, Wheatfield with Crows

stories.title: Keeping the Letter Beside the Image
stories.body:
Letter 898 describes the countryside and a group of paintings made in the final weeks at Auvers.  The letter is important because it preserves Vincent's own words. It does not name every canvas in the group or attach a single emotional meaning to each image.

The letter gives us a context for the late wheatfield group. It records how Vincent spoke about several paintings and his experience of the countryside. Read alongside this canvas, the passage opens a connection between his work and his words, with the precise relationship between an individual painting and each sentence still unresolved.
stories.prompt: What does the letter help you notice that the painting alone does not? What remains visible without the letter?

vgm-s0195v1962.title: Tree Roots
vgm-s0195v1962.collectionCredit: Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)
vgm-s0195v1962.labelTitle: A Painting Found in a Landscape
vgm-s0195v1962.body:
The canvas is filled by trunks, roots, slope and patches of colour. The ground rises close to the viewer, leaving little distance for a horizon. The painting asks for a near view. Our eyes move through a tangled field of relationships, searching for the boundaries between root, earth and shadow.

The Van Gogh Museum describes the work as unfinished and probably Vincent's final painting.  That wording preserves a conclusion with a boundary around it. It records the museum's assessment while leaving room for chronology to remain a research question.

In 2020, Wouter van der Veen proposed a location in Auvers by comparing the painting with a historical postcard. Later historical photographs strengthened the place-based investigation.  The location helps us understand what kind of slope and trees Vincent may have been observing. It does not turn the painting into a map of the events that followed.

A later family letter by Andries Bonger describes a forest scene painted on the morning before Vincent's death. This testimony has influenced the work's afterlife, although it was written after the event and does not identify the canvas with complete certainty.

The image remains close to the ground. Its history moves between material evidence, place research and later memory. Each layer adds information. None should be allowed to close the painting too quickly.

stories.title: From Pattern to Place
stories.body:
Wouter van der Veen proposed that the tangled forms correspond to a location in Auvers visible in a historical postcard. Later research and photographs supported further investigation of the site.  This is a historical identification, not a direct record of Vincent's route or a signed statement of intention.

The postcard, historical photographs and painting offer different records of a sloping place. Comparing the position of trunks, roots and exposed ground gives the proposal its substance. The investigation concerns where Vincent may have found his subject. It does not establish the location of the shooting, his route that day or the circumstances of his injury.

stories.title: A Postcard, Then a Photograph
stories.body:
The site story developed through research. A postcard prompted the 2020 proposal, and later historical images supplied additional context.  This is an example of how an artwork can generate new historical questions long after its creation.

A similar slope or tree line can support the identification of a landscape. The comparison still has limits: photographs record particular views at particular dates, and a painted view involves selection. Neither can recover every action that took place there or tell us exactly when each painted mark was made. The site proposal answers a question about the subject while leaving other parts of the final-days story unresolved.

stories.title: Why the Museum Says Probably
stories.body:
The Van Gogh Museum uses the word “probably” when describing Tree Roots as Vincent's final painting.  The word matters. It signals a strong institutional assessment that still retains uncertainty.

The story is also connected with a letter by Andries Bonger describing a sunlit forest scene painted before Vincent's death. The Van Gogh Museum discusses this account in connection with the painting.  Bonger's words are later testimony. They contribute to the reconstruction of chronology, with questions remaining about precisely which scene he meant and how his account relates to this canvas.

The museum's assessment, the family testimony and the site investigation are distinct parts of this history. Read together, they help explain why the painting occupies such an important place in accounts of Vincent's final days. Their remaining uncertainties also matter. The image cannot, on its own, establish his intentions or explain his death.

vgm-s0195v1962.evidence:
Institutionally documented: Title, date, medium, dimensions, object number, unfinished status and the museum's wording that it is probably the final painting.

Research history: The proposed site identification and subsequent historical-image research.

Later testimony: Andries Bonger’s account of a forest scene painted shortly before Vincent's death.

Curatorial reading: The painting's history demonstrates how place research, institutional caution and later memory can coexist without collapsing into a single death narrative.

Unknown: The exact completion date, whether the canvas was finished on the day described by later testimony, the identity of every visible tree, and any direct connection between the painted site and the shooting.
